Chapter 5: Facing Doubt and Skepticism—the Challenge of Believing in a Modern World
These days, it can honestly feel like believing in God means swimming upstream. We live in a world shaped by science and skepticism, where the only things that seem to count are the ones you can measure or prove. Anything that hints at the supernatural? It's often brushed off as superstition or wishful thinking. And if you find yourself longing for something more, you might feel pretty alone—or even a little bit ashamed.
Therapy rooms aren't shielded from these pressures, either. I often see clients walk in carrying both hope and hesitation. They're not sure if their spiritual experiences will be respected, or if they'll be seen as naïve. Maybe they've been told that faith means weakness, denial, or even childishness. That kind of message can really weigh you down—so now, you're not just dealing with your own pain, but also worrying you'll be dismissed or misunderstood.
But here's something to pay attention to—doubt isn't the enemy of faith. In fact, it can be the doorway to something much deeper. So many people who've had profound encounters with God started off with serious skepticism. They questioned, challenged, and wrestled with their beliefs. They refused to settle for easy answers, and it was right there—in the struggle—that they found something real. Something they couldn't just explain away.
Let me share a couple of stories. There was a man who grew up in a totally secular home. After losing someone he loved, he started searching for meaning. He dove into philosophy, science, religion—you name it—but nothing filled the hunger he felt for truth. Only when he got honest about his doubts, and brought them into conversation with God, did something shift. It wasn't dramatic, but it was unmistakable—a sense of being seen and known, even while he was still confused.
Then there was a woman, burned out by years of religious hypocrisy. She left faith behind and built a life on reason and self-reliance. But that ache for something more just wouldn’t go away. In therapy, she began to name the wounds—how people, claiming to speak for God, had hurt her. Slowly, she found the courage to separate her painful experiences with religion from the possibility of a living God. Over time, her faith grew into something deeper and more genuine than she’d ever known.
These stories really highlight something important: faith isn't about having zero doubts. It's about moving forward, even when things aren't certain. It's a journey, not just a destination—a process of asking questions, searching, sometimes stumbling along the way. For a lot of people, the most powerful moments with God don't come from certainty, but from wrestling with questions that don’t have easy answers.
So, what does this mean in therapy? It means making space for doubt—not as a problem to fix, but as a vital part of the journey. It takes real courage to ask hard questions, and it’s important to resist the urge to just hand out quick fixes or easy platitudes. Sometimes, that means grappling with suffering—wondering how a loving God could allow so much pain. Sometimes, it means confronting the failures of religious communities and figuring out how to trust again.
What comes out of all this? A faith that's humble and resilient. It's not about blind acceptance or rigid rules—it's about lived experience. It's knowing you've encountered something real, even when you're still wrestling with doubts. And that kind of faith? It's not threatened by tough questions. If anything, it grows stronger—more authentic—with every challenge.
In a world obsessed with certainty and control, this journey can feel risky. But if you're willing to take that leap, the rewards are profound. You discover a God who welcomes your questions, who meets you right in the middle of your struggles. And you find a faith that's not just a set of beliefs, but a living relationship—one that brings hope, healing, and transformation in ways that you can't always explain.
